name: Ceftriaxone

summary: Cephalosporin antibacterial for infections caused by susceptible organisms. Nursing focus: hypersensitivity history, calcium-containing solutions and diarrhoea.

items.text: The label advises obtaining specimens to identify the organism and its susceptibility before treatment, and indicates ceftriaxone for infections caused by susceptible organisms.

Ask about previous reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins and other beta-lactams before the first dose and report them; check with the pharmacy or prescriber before any calcium-containing solution is given at the same time.
Monitoring frequency and alarm limits follow the unit's protocol for this medicine.

The label states ceftriaxone must not be given through the same line at the same time as calcium-containing IV solutions (including continuous calcium-containing infusions such as parenteral nutrition), because a precipitate can form; in patients other than neonates the two may be given one after the other if the line is thoroughly flushed between them, but this is contraindicated outright in neonates aged 28 days or younger because of reports of fatal outcomes. The label also describes serious neurological adverse reactions reported with ceftriaxone, including encephalopathy (reduced consciousness, lethargy, confusion), seizures, myoclonus and non-convulsive status epilepticus; some cases occurred in patients with severe renal impairment who did not receive an appropriate dose adjustment.

Before therapy, careful inquiry should establish whether the patient has had hypersensitivity reactions to cephalosporins, penicillins and other beta-lactams, and the product should be given cautiously to beta-lactam-sensitive patients.
Serious acute hypersensitivity reactions may require emergency measures, and serious and occasionally fatal reactions have been reported with beta-lactams.

Ceftriaxone must never be given through the same line at the same time as calcium-containing IV solutions, in any age group, because of reports of fatal intravascular ceftriaxone-calcium precipitates, with neonates at the greatest risk.
The label describes ceftriaxone as generally well tolerated and lists local reactions, hypersensitivity and diarrhoea among the effects observed.
Stop and call for help for allergic signs; report severe or persistent diarrhoea.
Record the product and order checks, monitoring results, adverse events and escalation per unit standard.
Institution-specific preparation: follow your pharmacy's preparation standard and the product labelling. This library gives no preparation or concentration instructions.
Institution-specific dosing: follow the prescriber's order and your institution's approved protocol. This library gives no dosing instructions.

monitoring.text: Check beta-lactam allergy history before the first dose.
Watch for rash, breathing difficulty or swelling.
Check the site for local reactions.
Stop and report allergic signs immediately; also report confusion, reduced consciousness, or any seizure-like activity, especially in a patient with renal impairment.
Before giving ceftriaxone, confirm no calcium-containing solution (including parenteral nutrition) is running or about to run through the same line.
